I think money is a measure of little more than the successful pursuit of such. It does have loose correlations with some features of 'value' but in general the best way to earn money is to seek it out or to be granted it by birth. Now imagine we could ask any successful scientist if they'd had the mutually exclusive choice of being a successful scientist of moderate means or being a scientifically illiterate millionaire. Which do you think they'd pick? I imagine it'd be very near if not literally 100% on the path of science. And that, alone, is I think, the reason we have Boole the famed mathematician instead of a Boole the millionaire who nobody would know the name of today. I mean Boole started his own school at age 19! I don't think this is even speculation. If his pursuit were money instead of knowledge, I have little doubt he would have found success there as well. Thankfully for all, it was not.

I'll make myself clearer: everybody likes to enjoy a good living, and that costs money. So money is kind of a reward: do X and you'll have a comfortable life. Everything is in the X: is it talent? Leadership? Morality? Athleticity? The choice is in the society's hands. Therefore, society can pick and choose what kind of person to incentivize, in order to have more persons like that.

Now look at our society and ask yourself what its choice was. Definitely not "mathematical geniuses".

Money isn't some reward handed out to recognize achievement, nor does society arbitrarily pick and choose what's incentivized. When I give somebody 20 chickens for a suitable pig, I'm not giving them 20 chickens as a reward - but because I want the pig and they want the chickens. The value of anything is based largely primarily on the needs followed by the desires of people. Their needs and desires reflect nothing beyond that. Entertainment will always earn more than most things because it's not only a desire but arguably a need for humans.

You're not only forgetting laws and taxes, which heavily influence where money goes, but also how needs and desires are shaped by social customs, morality, ideology, and propaganda, especially advertising. This is what I meant by "society".

Let us take this away from the increasingly abstract and get back into the most realistic situation possible. I, ideologically, want to agree with your premise but I don't think it's logically sound. How would you formulate a logically coherent society such that brilliant mathematicians earned more than brilliant rappers (to ensure we are being fair)?

The only non-absurd way I can see of doing this is to formulate a society where rap is simply not popular but this says nothing about their valuing of mathematicians. Take yourself as an example. How much would you value your 30th favorite food compared to the funding of the education in the undeveloped world. I think most people would probably rank the education aspect vastly higher, yet have likely spent vastly more on the food. The point being that just because the social value of 'x' (e.g. math) is higher than 'y' (e.g. rap) does not necessarily mean that the monetary outcome of x will be greater than y.
